query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Short-range chemical ordering developing during moderate cooling from the high-temperature BCC state in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 creates local compositional fluctuations that serve as heterogeneous nucleation sites for secondary phase formation during subsequent thermal exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature, single-phase BCC state
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of samples differing only in cooling rate immediately after high-temperature processing – one set is rapidly quenched (minimizing atomic rearrangement) and the other is slowly cooled (allowing SRO to develop) – followed by identical thermal aging at an intermediate temperature (e.g., ~750°C) for a controlled time period.
generation.conditions: The hypothesis applies under processing conditions where the cooling rate is moderate enough to permit limited atomic diffusion and formation of short-range order but not so slow as to reach equilibrium; it should not apply when the cooling rate is so rapid that atomic rearrangements (and thus SRO) are completely suppressed or under processing routes dominated by non-equilibrium kinetics unrelated to ordering.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range chemical ordering (SRO) among key elements (notably interactions involving Al with Co, Ni, and Fe) that induces local free-energy minima.
generation.mechanism: During a slow cooling process, limited atomic mobility allows certain element pairs to transiently associate, lowering the local free energy and forming SRO regions. These chemically heterogeneous regions lower the nucleation barrier for secondary phases (e.g., ordered or precipitate phases) during subsequent moderate-temperature aging. In contrast, rapid cooling suppresses this rearrangement, preserving the high-temperature BCC state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Slow-cooled samples, after identical aging, should exhibit detectable secondary phases (via changes in diffraction peak patterns, emergence of nano-precipitates, or local compositional variations revealed by atom probe tomography), while rapidly quenched samples should remain predominantly single-phase BCC with minimal signs of SRO or secondary phase nucleation.
generation.baseline: Samples that are rapidly quenched from the high-temperature BCC state, thereby retaining a largely homogeneous BCC structure without significant SRO.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic pathway is expected to occur only when cooling rates allow atomic diffusion adequate for SRO formation yet are not fully equilibrating; conditions with extreme quenching or additional factors (e.g., imposed stresses, external fields) that dominate atomic mobility may fall outside the scope of this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: The precise identity, morphology, and volume fraction of the secondary phases remain uncertain. Moreover, quantifying the extent of SRO and its direct correlation with phase transformation kinetics requires further experimental clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples processed from the high-temperature BCC state: one set is rapidly quenched to suppress SRO formation and the other is slowly cooled to allow SRO development. Then, subject both sets to identical thermal aging at an intermediate temperature (e.g., ~750°C) for a fixed duration. Characterize the microstructure and phase composition using X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and atom probe tomography.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect emergence of new phase reflections or peak shifts indicative of phase transformation
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) imaging to identify nano-precipitates or ordered domains
Atom probe tomography (APT) to detect local chemical ordering and compositional fluctuations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, after aging, there is no statistically significant difference in the presence or extent of secondary phases or SRO between the slowly cooled and rapidly quenched samples, then the hypothesis that SRO drives secondary phase nucleation is falsified.

In this work, the aging behavior of a promising CCA for high-temperature application from WQ state to a maximum of 50 h aging at 750 °C is characterized by SEM, TEM, and APT measurements. The shape, size, and composition of the matrix and precipitate phases are determined and compared to Ni-based superalloys from the literature. Properties of individual phases have been studied using ab-initio-based model calculations supported by complementary experimental investigations. The following conclusions can be drawn from the results: After 10 h of aging at 750 °C, the majority of the thermodynamically stable γ’ ((Ni,Co)3(Al,Ti)) precipitates are formed. A comparison of the precipitate size after 50 h of aging with state-of-the-art Ni-based alloys from the literature suggests a comparatively low coarsening of the particles. Ni- and Ti-rich precipitates are observed in APT measurements of the WQ state, which already possess the stoichiometric ratio of the (Ni,Co)3(Al,Ti) γ’ phase. This indicates that it is nearly impossible to obtain a fully supersaturated and single-phased (ideal HEA) state in the selected CCA. One limitation of this study is the sheer number of ways the alloys could be processed in comparison with the methods utilized herein. Differences in processing (e.g., annealing temperature) can result in conflicting reports for the same composition (e.g., some Cantor alloys which are well known to decompose into multiple phases at lower temperatures). For example, the data compiled by Murty et al. lists 43 different processing routes. The caveat to the numerous processing routes is that several, such as sputtering, mechanical alloying, melt spinning, and suction casting, are known to allow for metastable structures. One such example in the dataset is CrNbTiVZn (60% BCC and 20% HEX non-allotropes) processed by 60 h of mechanical alloying and reported to be single phase FCC by Dwivedi et al.. In their own work, the authors recognize the metastable nature of the FCC phase achieved under non-equilibrium conditions. It is likely that other reports in the aggregated datasets are for non-equilibrium results.
